summary.summary: Westmorland and Furness closed 2025/26 with a quiet treasury position: no new external borrowing was taken, the council instead covering previously approved borrowing need from short-term cash reserves rather than paying for new loans. Debt stood at £173.6m (average rate 3.7%) against £74.6m of temporary investments (average 4.07%) at 31 March 2026, and treasury management came in £6.3m under its £14.65m budget thanks to high interest earned on retained cash balances. The report confirms all treasury activity complied with the prudential indicators and the February 2025 strategy. Full Council was also asked to approve a revised 2025-2031 capital programme of £591.1m at outturn, up from £432.1m when first set in February 2025, with outturn slippage of £10.1m and accelerated spend of £12.6m.

signals.why: A council funding its capital programme from cash rather than new loans, with treasury costs well under budget, presents no near-term treasury concerns for a lender.

compliance.notes: A strong core TMSS: five-year prudential indicator suite, a 13-year four-balance liability benchmark, a CDS-informed creditworthiness policy and a well-reasoned borrowing strategy. Weakest areas are commercial/non-treasury disclosure (proportionality recited but never quantified, no PI-08 ratio, no IMPs, no exit/fair-value substance) and formal governance hooks (no four-clause adoption statement, scrutiny committee unnamed); indicator tables omit prior-year actuals throughout, and the capital strategy in force dates from June 2024 with the 2026/27 refresh still in draft at TMSS time. Scored from the council-website final versions because the moderngov packet URLs (s40871/s37305) sit behind a Cloudflare challenge.

news_drafts.headline: Westmorland and Furness capital forecast shows £4.818m slippage on high needs school provision
news_drafts.lead:
Westmorland and Furness Council's first-quarter forecast for 2026/27, put to the full council on 24 September, shows £4.818m of slippage on its high needs school provision. It is the largest deferral of any single scheme in the council's capital programme. The capital programme is the council's planned spending on things that last, such as buildings, roads and equipment. High needs is the part of school funding that supports children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND).

The scheme had a forecast of £2.876m for the year. After the slippage, the 2026/27 budget for it is £1.0m. Slippage means spending planned for one year is now expected to fall later.

The appendix to the report sets out the figures scheme by scheme, and the high needs line is the biggest movement among them. The material available does not give the reason for the deferral.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for WFC 24/09 - Capital Programme Forecast Q1 26/27
findings.headline: A595 Grizebeck Stage 2 deferred by £3.5m, reducing major trans-Pennine route investment from £8.6m to £5.1m.
findings.detail: The A595 Grizebeck Stage 2 (strategic route connecting South Lakes through Barrow northward) shows (£3.500m) slippage from a £8.568m budget. The scheme is not progressing on the planned timescale, leaving £5.068m budgeted for 2026/27.
findings.matters: Major transport infrastructure delays affect regional economic connectivity; slippage signals either procurement challenges, environmental hold-ups, or delivery capacity constraints, relevant to the council's highways asset management and long-term infrastructure strategy.
findings.figures: A595 Grizebeck Stage 2: £8.568m budget, (£3.500m) slippage, £5.068m revised forecast

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for WFC 24/09 - Capital Programme Forecast Q1 26/27
findings.headline: Levelling Up Fund schemes totalling £4.0m deferred in-year: Barrow Market (£2.0m), Kendal (£1.4m), Eden Hub (£0.7m).
findings.detail: Three Levelling Up Fund regeneration schemes are being significantly pushed to 2027/28: Barrow Market & Public Realm (£2.008m), Heart of Kendal (£1.366m), and Eden Enterprise Hub (£0.658m). These are government-backed initiatives with defined spend windows and grant conditions.
findings.matters: Levelling Up grants have spend timescales and clawback provisions; failure to deliver to schedule or meet grant conditions can result in fund recovery, affecting the council's financial position and place-making objectives.
findings.figures: Barrow LUF (£2.008m), Kendal LUF (£1.366m), Eden Hub LUF (£0.658m); combined deferral £4.032m
findings.quote: Levelling Up Fund - Barrow Market & Public Realm 5.008 (2.008) 3.000; Heart of Kendal 1.616 (1.366) 0.250; Levelling Up Fund - Eden Enterprise Hub 0.758 (0.658) 0.100

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for WFC 24/09 - Capital Programme Forecast Q1 26/27
findings.headline: High Needs provision deferred by £4.8m—the single largest scheme slippage—leaving only £1.0m budgeted for rest of year.
findings.detail: High Needs school provision (SEND pupils) shows (£4.818m) slippage from a £2.876m forecast, reducing 2026/27 budget to £1.0m. This is the largest individual scheme deferral in the entire programme. SEND provision pressures are a national pattern, with most councils managing waiting lists and insufficient places.
findings.matters: SEND need is a structural budget pressure for councils; inability to deliver planned provision signals either changing demand (a future cost pressure) or commissioning and delivery difficulties that may extend to wider capital execution.
findings.figures: High Needs Provision: £2.876m forecast, (£4.818m) slippage, £1.0m revised forecast for 2026/27

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for WFC 24/09 - Capital Programme Forecast Q1 26/27
findings.headline: Capital programme slippage of £27.992m (20% of budget) defers schemes from 2026/27 to future years.
findings.detail: The council's total capital programme budget was reduced from £139.3m to £114.0m through £28.0m of slippage. Slippage is concentrated in High Needs education (£4.8m), major infrastructure (A595 Grizebeck £3.5m, LEVI £1.8m), Levelling Up Fund schemes (£4.0m), and highways. This represents schemes being pushed into 2027/28 and beyond rather than spending as planned.
findings.matters: Programme slippage at 20% scale signals either over-optimistic budgeting, resource or procurement constraints, or strategic reprioritisation; lenders assess this as a measure of the council's capital execution capability and ability to deliver planned investment.
findings.figures: (£27.992m) slippage; revised budget falls from £139.328m to £113.994m

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for WFC 24/09 - Capital Programme Changes Q1 26/27
findings.headline: The council has reproffiled £27.992m of planned 2026/27 capital expenditure to future years in Q1, reducing the directly delivered programme from £130.497m to £113.994m.
findings.detail: Multiple schemes have been moved back from 2026/27, including A595 Grizebeck Stage 2 (£3.5m), High Needs Provision (£4.8m), Modernising the Estate (£1m), and various Levelling Up Fund and Town Deal schemes. Most reproffiled spend is being pushed to 2027/28, which means planned asset delivery and associated benefits are being deferred.
findings.matters: A lender would want to understand whether the council can deliver its planned capital investment as intended and whether spending profiles are predictable, both of which affect cash flow, borrowing requirements, and the pace of asset investment.
findings.figures: Total reproffiling Q1 2026/27: £27.992m; Originally approved 2026/27: £130.497m; After reproffiling: £113.994m (reduction of 12.6%); A595 Grizebeck Stage 2 £3.500m; High Needs Provision £4.818m
